title: Regina Caeli
hook: in Eastertide it replaces the Angelus: rejoice, he is risen

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ave Regina Caelorum, the night song of Lent, with its goodbye before sleep. Your line was hail, queen of heaven.

Noon, and somewhere a church bell rings. For much of the year, the prayer that goes with that bell is the Angelus, which you met on day one hundred three: an angel, a young woman, a yes, and the Word made flesh. But from Easter to Pentecost, Catholics who keep the noon bell set the Angelus aside and pray something else. The story has jumped to its ending, and the prayer jumps with it. It's short, and every line ends in the same word, like a door that keeps swinging open: alleluia. Today's word is the Easter prayer to Mary, Regina Caeli.
screen: `NOON, AND A BELL.` → `THE ANGELUS TELLS THE BEGINNING.` → `IN EASTER, THE ENDING.`

segments.voice: In plain English: queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia. For he whom you were worthy to bear, alleluia, has risen, as he said, alleluia. Pray for us to God, alleluia. Start with the first command: rejoice, in Latin laetare. Think back this week to the woman who stood at the cross, whose soul Simeon said a sword would pierce. In the Easter prayer, the first thing said to her is be glad. The one who knew the worst of Friday is told about Sunday. Then the two Latin words in the middle that carry the weight: sicut dixit, as he said. They echo the angel at the empty tomb in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "He is not here, for he is risen, as he said." The prayer doesn't only announce that he rose. It says he kept his word. A promise made before the cross turns out true on the other side of it. Then the alleluias. Through Lent, the Latin Church sets the word alleluia aside; it isn't sung at Mass. At Easter it comes back, and this little prayer can't stop saying it. Last, it still asks: pray for us to God. Even at the height of joy, it turns to Mary for help, the way this whole week has. So in Easter the noon bell rings for a mother told to rejoice because her son kept his promise.
screen: `THE FIRST WORD TO HER: REJOICE.` · `SICUT DIXIT: AS HE SAID.` · `ALLELUIA COMES BACK.` · `STILL ASKING: PRAY FOR US.` · then, large: `HE IS NOT HERE, FOR HE IS RISEN, AS HE SAID.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise someone made to you and kept, a friend who showed up, a call returned, and remember the moment you knew they'd kept it; then let it widen: as he said. If you pray, say the Regina Caeli slowly now, with an alleluia at the end of each line. If you don't, hold that kept promise in mind and let it be good news.

Regina Caeli. Queen of heaven: the Easter prayer, rejoice, he is risen. This week's road: many names, poetry for a mother, comfort of the afflicted, mother of the church, star of the sea, hail, queen of heaven, and now rejoice.
Your line: queen of heaven, rejoice. He kept his word. Alleluia, and see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In the Easter season, from Easter to Pentecost, Catholics who pray the Angelus at morning, noon and evening say the Regina Caeli in its place, and it also closes Night Prayer through that season.

chat.says: What's the big deal about 'as he said' in the Regina Caeli?
options: It echoes the angel at the tomb: Jesus rose as he promised. The prayer says he kept his word.
It means Mary predicted the resurrection herself, and the prayer credits her for saying so.
It's a polite filler phrase in Latin, added so the lines rhyme before each alleluia.
chat.meaning: Sicut dixit echoes Matthew 28:6, 'he is risen, as he said': the prayer tells Mary her son kept his promise.

Angelus.meaning: the noon prayer telling of the angel's visit to Mary

alleluia.meaning: a cry of praise, set aside in Lent and sung again at Easter

Pentecost.meaning: the coming of the Holy Spirit, which ends the Easter season
